solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Whizz outclasses those without hope of success

indicators.note: to whizz is to whirl around at speed, so the following word is spun into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written, all ten letters used

explanation.surface: A star performer so dominant that the rivals are left with no chance of winning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whizz' reads as a noun for a brilliant person, but it is the signal to rearrange OUTCLASSES into LOST CAUSES.
explanation.definitionFit: A lost cause is a person or project with no chance of succeeding, so the plural describes a group doomed to fail.

clue.text: Drinks rounds?

blocks.note: first meaning: a verb for lapping up liquid, as a cat does
second meaning: circuits of a running track

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests buying rounds of drinks in a pub; in fact one sense is a cat's lapping, the other is circuits of a track.
explanation.definitionFit: A cat drinking with its tongue does so with a verb meaning lick up, and a single circuit of a racetrack is called the same word.

clue.text: Outfits about to transport free trousers to Oz

indicators.note: about means turned around, so the word for outfits is read from the end back
to transport something is to carry it, so the outfits carry the word for free inside them

blocks.note: sets of clothes, or groups, are outfits
to rid is to free, as in rid of a burden

explanation.surface: Someone sorting out clothing for a trip down under, packing trousers.
explanation.walkthrough: Oz is Australia, where trousers are informally called strides; the word for outfits turns round and carries the word for free inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: In Australian slang trousers are known by the word for long walking paces, a usage the clue flags with its mention of Oz.

clue.text: One might get used to Polish vehicles

definitions.text: One might get used to Polish vehicles

blocks.note: surface reading: cars or buses made in Poland that someone gets accustomed to

blocks.clueFragment: One might get used to Polish vehicles
blocks.note: setter's reading: a soft cloth put to use to polish cars

explanation.walkthrough: The capital P makes it look like Poland; read it as the verb polish and the clue describes the cloth used to buff a car.
explanation.definitionFit: Chammy (chamois) leather is a soft absorbent cloth traditionally used for drying and polishing car paintwork and windows.

clue.text: Sherpa possibly less than enthralled climbing mountain

indicators.note: in a down entry climbing means going upward, so the word for mountain is read bottom to top
enthralled means held captive, so one word holds the other inside it

blocks.note: under means below or less than
an alp is a high mountain

explanation.surface: A Sherpa on a climb who is not entirely captivated by the mountain.
explanation.walkthrough: Climbing works twice: it suits the Sherpa in the surface, and in a down entry it sends the mountain upward.
explanation.definitionFit: Sherpas live in the high Himalayan regions of Nepal, so one is an example of a person from hill country.

clue.text: Call for Congress to reject second bill

indicators.note: rejecting something means throwing it out, so the letter for second is removed

blocks.note: congress can mean sexual intercourse
S is the abbreviation for second
a parliamentary bill becomes an act once passed

explanation.surface: A demand that the US Congress throw out a newly tabled piece of legislation.
explanation.walkthrough: Congress here is not the US legislature but sexual intercourse, an old formal sense of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: To exact is to demand or insist on something, such as payment or obedience, which is what calling for it means.

clue.text: Item that’ll stop dog biting end of tail

indicators.note: end of picks out only the final letter of the following word
something biting closes its jaws around a thing, so the dog word holds the letter inside

blocks.note: a pug is a small breed of dog
the last letter of tail

explanation.surface: A dog chewing at its own tail, and something that might put a stop to it.
explanation.walkthrough: PUG takes L in its mouth: P(L)UG.
explanation.definitionFit: A plug is a stopper fitted into a hole, such as a bath drain, to block flow.

clue.text: Family stays in Battle for short visits

indicators.note: something that stays in a place remains inside it, so the family word goes within the battle

blocks.note: Loos was a 1915 First World War battle in northern France
kin are relatives

explanation.surface: A family lodging in the East Sussex town of Battle, popping in on people briefly.
explanation.walkthrough: Battle is also a town near Hastings, which is the misdirection; the battle wanted is a 1915 one in France.
explanation.definitionFit: A look-in is informal British English for a brief call on someone, so the plural means quick visits.

clue.text: Young male lead seen with new flapper

blocks.note: green means inexperienced or young
the male lead in a story is its hero
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: A young actor playing the romantic lead opposite a 1920s flapper girl.
explanation.walkthrough: Flapper suggests a jazz-age young woman; here it simply means a thing that flaps its wings.
explanation.definitionFit: The green heron is a small American wading bird, and any bird beats its wings, so it is jokingly a flapper.

clue.text: Jumpy soldier capturing Malta’s city

indicators.note: a soldier capturing someone takes them in, so the soldier word surrounds Malta's letter

blocks.note: a para is a paratrooper, a soldier who jumps from aircraft
M is the international vehicle code for Malta

explanation.surface: A nervous soldier taking a Maltese town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumpy' looks like nervous, but it describes a parachutist. PARA holds M: PAR(M)A.
explanation.definitionFit: Parma is a northern Italian city, famous for its ham and cheese.

clue.text: Highly offensive males too awful, husband admitted

indicators.note: awful means dreadful, suggesting the preceding words are mangled into another order
admitted means let in, so the husband letter goes inside the rearranged letters

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: Complaining that men are dreadful, with a husband let in on it.
explanation.definitionFit: Loathsome describes something that causes disgust or hatred, which is to say extremely objectionable.

clue.text: Sadly, her noon habits can be absurdly complex

indicators.note: sadly suggests things have gone badly wrong, so the following letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written, all thirteen letters used

explanation.surface: A woman's midday routines are, unfortunately, ridiculously elaborate.
explanation.walkthrough: W. Heath Robinson was a British cartoonist who drew comically elaborate machines for simple tasks; his name became an adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: In British usage a Heath Robinson contraption is an ingenious but ludicrously overcomplicated device, after the cartoonist's drawings.

clue.text: Familiar bit of research in office presentation

indicators.note: a bit of a word is a small part of it, here its opening letter
in places the selected letter inside the word for office

blocks.note: a familiar is a witch's attendant spirit, a demon
a station is a post or position held, an office
the first letter of research

explanation.surface: Showing a familiar piece of research during a talk at work.
explanation.walkthrough: Familiar is the noun for a witch's attendant spirit, not the adjective meaning well known.
explanation.definitionFit: A demonstration is a practical display showing how something works, which is a kind of presentation to an audience.

clue.text: Youth succeeded in breaking local news

indicators.note: breaking smashes things apart, so these letters are reassembled differently

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for succeeded
taken as written

explanation.surface: A young person made good by breaking a story in the local paper.
explanation.walkthrough: S joins the nine letters of LOCAL NEWS and all ten are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Callowness is the inexperience and immaturity typical of the young, so it stands for youth in that sense.

clue.text: I will forgive a British person like yourself

definitions.note: a phrase spoken by the answer, standing for the noun

blocks.note: taken as written
B is the abbreviation for British
you, the reader, are someone working out the clues

explanation.surface: A British person promises to pardon you.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue addresses the solver directly, a favourite crossword trick.
explanation.definitionFit: An absolver is one who pardons or grants remission of sins, so such a person can say they will grant pardon.

clue.text: Pure heroin smuggled by group from India

indicators.note: something smuggled is hidden inside a carrier, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: a caste is a hereditary social class in Hindu India
H is slang for heroin

explanation.surface: Uncut heroin being trafficked by a gang from India.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pure' sits naturally with heroin in the surface, but it is the definition, in its moral sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Chaste means morally pure, especially abstaining from sexual activity.

clue.text: Prisoner at liberty to ring Republican brother at work

indicators.note: to ring is to encircle, so the word for at liberty surrounds the party letter

blocks.note: con is short for convict
free means not imprisoned
R is the abbreviation for Republican

explanation.surface: A released prisoner phones his Republican brother at the office.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer borrows French: frère is brother, and the English word keeps that sense of fellowship.
explanation.definitionFit: A confrere is a colleague or fellow member of a profession, a brother in the working sense.

clue.text: African seen in Bali by a Norwegian

indicators.note: seen in says the letters are visible inside the following words

blocks.note: found running across these words
N is the abbreviation for Norwegian

explanation.surface: A traveller from Africa spotted on holiday in Bali by someone from Norway.
explanation.definitionFit: A Libyan comes from Libya in North Africa, so the word names a kind of African person.

clue.text: Dash about, getting ambassador something for lunch?

blocks.note: brio means vigour or dash
C is short for circa, about
HE stands for His Excellency, an ambassador's title

explanation.surface: Rushing around to fetch an ambassador's meal.
explanation.walkthrough: Dash looks like a verb for hurrying, but it means flair. The question mark admits brioche is more often eaten at breakfast.
explanation.definitionFit: Brioche is a rich sweet bread, which could be eaten at a midday meal, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Turn red, having left uni performance in a state

indicators.note: having left means having gone away, so the letter for university departs

blocks.note: to colour is to blush
U is the abbreviation for university
a performance is a fuss, an ado

explanation.surface: Someone blushing after walking out of a university show.
explanation.walkthrough: Dropping U from COLOUR gives the American spelling COLOR, fitting for a US state.
explanation.definitionFit: Colorado is one of the fifty United States, in the Rocky Mountains.

clue.text: National record sent up in article repeatedly

indicators.note: in a down entry sent up means moved upward, reading the record word backwards
in places the record inside the repeated article

blocks.note: an is the indefinite article, used twice
a log is a written record

explanation.surface: A national record mocked repeatedly in a newspaper piece.
explanation.walkthrough: Sent up suggests satirised, but in a down entry it means the record word is reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: An Angolan is a citizen of Angola, and the noun national means a citizen of a particular country.

clue.text: We fit lighting out setting bars up

indicators.note: out can mean wrong or askew, so these letters need rearranging

blocks.note: taken as written, all thirteen letters used

explanation.surface: Electricians installing lights while putting up bars in a pub.
explanation.walkthrough: Setting bars up sounds like fitting out a pub, but it is lifting barbells.
explanation.definitionFit: Weightlifting is the sport of raising a loaded barbell overhead, so it consists of hoisting bars.

clue.text: Will time off from work cause split?

blocks.note: first meaning: to bequeath something in a will
second meaning: an absence permitted by an employer
surface padding that hints at a third sense, to depart, which can end a relationship

explanation.surface: Wondering whether a holiday might lead to a break-up.
explanation.walkthrough: The tail 'cause split?' plays on a third sense, to depart, which can cause a split between people.
explanation.definitionFit: To will property is to pass it on at death, and a permitted absence from employment is also known by this word.

clue.text: Pull out your gun and charge in the wrong direction

indicators.note: going the wrong way means the letters are read back to front

blocks.note: a ward is a person placed in someone's charge

explanation.surface: A gunfighter who draws and rushes off the wrong way.
explanation.walkthrough: Charge looks like a rush or attack; it is a person in someone's care.
explanation.definitionFit: To draw a gun is to take it out of its holster, ready to fire.

clue.text: English No 10 I had put on my strip

indicators.note: put on means placed after, so the words for I had follow the exclamation

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
X is the Roman numeral for ten
cor is a British exclamation of surprise, like my!
taken as written
to have a meal is to eat it

explanation.surface: An English footballer wearing the number ten shirt.
explanation.walkthrough: No 10 suggests Downing Street or a shirt number; it is just the Roman ten.
explanation.definitionFit: To excoriate is literally to strip away the skin, and figuratively to criticise someone harshly.

clue.text: Mogul ultimately involved in rise of The Sun

indicators.note: ultimately means at the end, so only the last letter of the word is kept
involved in means drawn inside, so that letter is put within the word for rise

blocks.note: to soar is to rise high
the last letter of Mogul

explanation.surface: A media mogul behind the growth of The Sun newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun reads as Murdoch's tabloid; here it is the star. L goes into SOAR: SO(L)AR.
explanation.definitionFit: Solar is the adjective describing things belonging to or coming from our star.

clue.text: Action making dogs possibly run the other way?

indicators.note: running the other way means the letters go from end to start

blocks.note: dogs are an example of pets

explanation.surface: Something that might make dogs turn tail and flee.
explanation.definitionFit: A step is a measure taken to achieve something, as in taking steps, so it means an action.

clue.text: He warned, “no going out for the time being”

indicators.note: going out suggests things are disordered or off, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written, all ten letters used

explanation.surface: A parent's warning that there will be no nights out for now.
explanation.definitionFit: Here and now means at the present moment, which is the period covered by the phrase about the current time.
